01-introduction.name: 01-introduction
01-introduction.title: The workflow
captions: Before we build anything, let's make the
workflow clear. A chat response is useful
when you need an explanation, a first
draft or a second opinion, but some
work becomes easier when the answer has
controls. If you keep asking for the
same calculation with a different number, that
number probably belongs in an input.
If you keep asking for the same
output in another format, that format probably
deserves an export button.
And if you keep copying an answer
somewhere else to finish the task, the
interface should help you reach that next
step. On screen, you can see four
examples I've prepared for this tutorial.
They use sample information and run locally
in the browser.
The first is a newsletter editor, the
second is a task organizer, the third
is a revenue model, and the fourth
is a packaging concept sheet.
These examples are separate from the AI
chat itself. The AI can help write
the code, and the browser runs the
resulting tool. That distinction matters because a
button that says send does not automatically
mean it has permission to send a
message, and a number on a dashboard
is only as good as the formula
behind it. We're going to work through
a simple pattern.
First, describe the task and the person
using the tool.
Second, specify the inputs and the output.
Third, identify the checks that would convince
us it works.
Then build a small version, use it,
and ask for targeted improvements.
For the newsletter, our input is a
subject line and a draft.
The output is something we can copy
or export. Our checks are straightforward.
The preview should match our text, the
word count should change as we type,
and the exported file should preserve what
we wrote. For the revenue model, the
checks are mathematical.
We'll use a simple example that we
can calculate ourselves, then compare it with
the screen. You don't need to request
a huge application to get value from
this approach. In fact, the first useful
version is often one page with a
few controls. Keep the scope small enough
that you can understand what happens when
you click, and add complexity only after
the basic workflow is reliable.
Let's use the newsletter to put that
into practice.

02-newsletter-build.name: 02-newsletter-build
02-newsletter-build.title: Newsletter: build the editor
captions: Let’s start with the problem this editor
solves. You have a newsletter draft, and
you want to improve it without bouncing
between a chat, a document, a word
counter, and an export tool.
The point of the interface is to
put the repeated decisions in one place.
On the left, we change the subject
and body, and on the right, we
see the result.
The controls should be obvious enough that
somebody who never saw the original prompt
can still use the page.
Here is how I would describe this
to an AI.
Build a single-page newsletter editor with an
editable subject and body, a live preview,
word count, reading-time estimate, local autosave, and
downloads in useful formats.
Use sample text and keep it independent
of external services.
That is a much more useful request
than simply asking for an amazing newsletter
app, because each feature corresponds to something
we can inspect.
We can also tell the AI which
things it should not pretend to do,
such as sending the email or connecting
to our subscribers.
The recorded Claude build shows that process
from the prompt to a generated artifact.
The finished examples we use for the
detailed walkthrough are local tutorial files, so
you can inspect the same workflows without
needing a connected mailing list.
Different AI tools may produce different layouts
from the same brief, and that is
fine. What matters is whether the behavior
meets the brief.
A beautiful preview with broken downloads is
still an unfinished tool.
Start by changing the subject line.
Notice that this is ordinary editing, rather
than another instruction to the AI.
The preview responds immediately because the page
already knows how to handle that input.
Now change a sentence in the body.
Again, we do not need to send
the whole draft back to a model
merely to update the preview.
This is the useful division of labor:
the AI helps construct the tool, and
the tool handles the repeated mechanical work.
There is one important boundary here.
This editor does not automatically improve your
writing. It displays and exports what you
enter. If you want an AI rewrite
button, that becomes another feature with its
own connection, cost, privacy choices, and error
handling. We are deliberately starting with the
reliable local workflow.
You can ask an AI to help
revise a paragraph separately, paste the version
you prefer, and keep control of the
final wording. Before adding more features, ask
whether the current screen already removes a
step from your work.
If the answer is yes, you have
a useful first version.
The next step is to test the
feedback and exports, because those are what
make this more than a visual mockup.

03-newsletter-checks.name: 03-newsletter-checks
03-newsletter-checks.title: Newsletter: test and export
captions: Now we’ll check the editor using a
deliberately small example.
Replace the body with ten simple words,
and compare the displayed count with the
actual text. A tiny example is easier
to verify than a long article, and
it helps us separate a working feature
from a number that merely looks plausible.
The count in this tutorial uses words
separated by whitespace, so punctuation attached to
a word does not create an extra
word. More sophisticated editors may use different
rules, especially across languages.
The reading-time estimate is also transparent.
This version divides the word count by
two hundred words per minute.
That is a convenient assumption for the
demonstration, not a measurement of how every
subscriber reads. A technical newsletter may take
longer because the reader stops to think.
An image-heavy newsletter has information that a
simple word counter cannot capture.
Keep the assumption visible so the estimate
is useful without pretending to be exact.
Next, restore the sample draft and add
a short practical takeaway.
The preview should match what we typed,
including paragraph breaks.
Then check the local-save message.
Local autosave means the draft is stored
in this browser on this device.
It does not mean the draft has
been backed up to your account or
synchronized across a team.
If you clear browser storage or switch
profiles, the saved text may not follow
you. For anything important, use an export
as well. The plain-text output is useful
when you want the content without formatting.
Markdown is useful when your next tool
understands lightweight headings and paragraphs.
The HTML export is useful for inspecting
a formatted document, but you still need
to test it in the actual email
system you intend to use.
A browser page and an email client
do not necessarily render the same way.
The export is a starting point for
that handoff, not proof that every inbox
will display it perfectly.
We also need to test text that
resembles markup. If I type angle brackets
into a draft, the exported document should
display that text rather than treating it
as executable content.
This is why the brief asked for
escaping user content.
You do not need to memorize the
implementation to request the behavior and test
the result. Finally, think about one focused
improvement. Perhaps you need a subject-length indicator
or a second preview size.
Ask for that one change, explain the
expected result, and repeat the original checks
afterward. A revision can accidentally break something
that already worked.
The habit we want is simple: build
a small tool, use a small test,
and keep the useful behavior intact as
you improve it.

04-task-board.name: 04-task-board
04-task-board.title: Tasks: make the next action clear
captions: Our second example starts with a familiar
problem: a task list that keeps growing
even though nobody is clear about the
next action. A longer list does not
necessarily create more clarity.
We want an interface that forces a
useful decision, so this board has four
destinations: do now, schedule, delegate, and drop.
Those labels are choices for this demonstration,
and you can adapt them to the
way your team actually works.
Look at the sample tasks.
Reviewing a landing-page headline may be something
you can do now.
Planning a tutorial may need a deliberate
block of time.
Resizing campaign images may be appropriate to
delegate. Rebuilding a report nobody uses may
deserve a conversation about whether it should
happen at all.
The board makes those alternatives visible instead
of treating every task as equally urgent.
Each task also has an estimate in
minutes. These estimates are not promises, and
the app does not know how long
the work will really take.
Their purpose is to make capacity visible.
A column with ten tasks can look
manageable until you notice that it represents
six hours of work.
Adding the estimates gives you another way
to challenge the plan before you commit
to it. Now add a new task
with a clear action in its name.
Instead of writing website, write review the
homepage call to action.
A task should tell somebody what to
do, and ideally what result would count
as done. Enter an estimate, add it
to the board, and move it to
the right destination.
Watch the totals update as the task
changes columns. This is exactly the kind
of repetitive bookkeeping that a small interface
can handle for us.
There is a useful test here.
Move one thirty-minute task from do now
to delegate. The first total should go
down by thirty, and the second should
go up by thirty.
The overall amount of estimated work should
not change merely because we moved a
card. If those numbers do not agree,
stop and fix the tool before relying
on it for a real planning session.
This first version uses sample tasks and
keeps the workflow simple.
It does not synchronize with your project-management
system, invite teammates, or infer priorities from
private messages. Those would be separate integrations.
You can still get value immediately by
using the board to organize a short
planning conversation, then transferring the agreed actions
into the system your team already uses.
The important design question is what happens
after the sorting.
A board that only looks organized may
not change the work.
In the next step, we’ll take the
delegate column and turn it into a
clear message that a person can review
and send.

05-delegation.name: 05-delegation
05-delegation.title: Tasks: prepare a delegation draft
captions: Let’s turn the delegated tasks into a
usable handoff. The first input is the
teammate, and the second is the deadline.
Neither should be guessed silently.
The person receiving the work needs to
know what you are asking, when it
is needed, and whether you expect them
to confirm capacity.
For this example, we are using Alex
and a Friday deadline, but these are
sample details rather than a message to
a real colleague.
When we build the message, the tool
takes the tasks currently in the delegate
column and lists them with their estimates.
Read the result carefully.
It is a draft, and nothing has
been sent to Slack.
The copy button makes it easier to
move the text to the place where
you normally communicate, but copying is different
from sending. Keeping that distinction visible prevents
the interface from suggesting an integration that
does not exist.
A useful delegation message should also describe
the desired outcome.
If the task is to resize campaign
images, you might specify the required sizes,
the source folder, and where the finished
exports belong. Our small example does not
contain all that context, so the person
sending the message should add it.
The app can reduce formatting work, but
it cannot replace the judgment needed to
make a good handoff.
Now move another task into the delegate
column and rebuild the draft.
Compare the message with the board.
Every listed task should be one you
actually intended to delegate, and a task
moved out of that column should disappear
when you rebuild.
This is an easy place for generated
tools to get something wrong if they
keep a stale copy of the task
list. Testing the change is more informative
than only testing the initial sample.
Also test the empty case.
If there are no delegated tasks, a
helpful tool should say so.
It should not generate an empty assignment
that looks ready to send.
Small empty states matter because real work
does not always arrive in the perfect
shape used in a demonstration.
If you later connect this workflow to
a messaging service, design a review step
before the send action.
Show the destination, recipient, and final text.
Make success and failure visible, and avoid
sending the same message twice if a
request times out.
Those are requirements you can put in
the brief even if you are not
writing the integration yourself.
For now, the useful result is a
reviewed draft. We have taken a vague
list, made decisions about the next actions,
and produced a concrete handoff.
That is the pattern to notice: the
interface should help the work move forward,
and it should be honest about where
the human decision still belongs.

06-revenue-model.name: 06-revenue-model
06-revenue-model.title: Revenue: check the calculations
captions: The third example is a revenue model,
and here the priority is transparency.
A slider is only useful if we
understand what changes when we move it.
We will use sample business assumptions and
simple arithmetic, then check the results ourselves.
This is a teaching model, not a
forecast of a real business, and we
are not giving the numbers a confidence
score they have not earned.
Start with twenty thousand monthly visitors, a
two percent conversion rate, and an average
order value of two hundred and fifty
dirhams. Two percent of twenty thousand gives
four hundred orders.
Multiply four hundred by two hundred and
fifty, and the revenue is one hundred
thousand dirhams. Those are the first two
checks we can perform without trusting the
interface. Now add a gross margin of
sixty percent and fixed monthly costs of
thirty thousand dirhams.
Sixty percent of one hundred thousand is
sixty thousand, and subtracting the fixed costs
leaves thirty thousand.
The label on screen describes this as
contribution after fixed costs.
It is not a complete accounting statement,
because the simplified model may leave out
taxes, financing, returns, and other items that
matter to an actual business.
The benefit of the interface is that
we can change an assumption and immediately
see the mechanical effect.
Increase the conversion rate from two percent
to three percent while keeping everything else
the same. Orders become six hundred, revenue
becomes one hundred and fifty thousand, and
the result after the costs in this
model becomes sixty thousand.
That does not prove we can achieve
a three percent conversion rate.
It shows what the formula would produce
if that assumption were true.
Now reduce conversion to one percent.
Orders fall to two hundred, revenue falls
to fifty thousand, and sixty percent of
that revenue exactly covers the thirty thousand
in fixed costs.
This gives us a useful check: under
these particular assumptions, one percent is the
break-even conversion rate for the costs included
here. Change the costs or margin and
that break-even point will change too.
Notice how different this is from repeatedly
asking a chat to calculate another scenario.
Once the formula is in a working
tool, we can explore it directly.
The AI was useful for helping construct
the interface, but each slider movement is
just a calculation in the browser.
That makes the result easy to inspect,
repeat, and explain to somebody else.
Before using a model like this in
a meeting, write down where each assumption
came from. A real visitor count, a
historical conversion rate, and a guess about
future order value should not be presented
as equally certain.
The interface can make arithmetic faster, but
the evidence behind the inputs still determines
whether the discussion is useful.

07-scenarios.name: 07-scenarios
07-scenarios.title: Revenue: compare scenarios
captions: Let’s look at the scenario table rather
than a single headline number.
In this example, the conservative scenario reduces
the conversion assumption by twenty-five percent, the
base case leaves it unchanged, and the
stretch scenario increases it by twenty-five percent.
We are changing only conversion.
The other inputs stay fixed so that
we can see exactly where the difference
comes from. With a base conversion rate
of two percent, those scenarios become one
and a half percent, two percent, and
two and a half percent.
That is a relative change of twenty-five
percent, not an increase or decrease of
twenty-five percentage points.
The distinction matters, because those two phrases
describe very different calculations.
A good interface should make this assumption
visible rather than hiding it behind attractive
scenario names. Using our sample visitor count
and order value, the revenue numbers become
seventy-five thousand, one hundred thousand, and one
hundred and twenty-five thousand dirhams.
After applying the same margin and fixed
costs, the corresponding results are fifteen thousand,
thirty thousand, and forty-five thousand.
Take a moment to compare the table
with those calculations.
We want the numbers to be boringly
consistent. Next, change the fixed costs while
leaving the sales assumptions alone.
Revenue should remain unchanged, because fixed costs
do not enter the revenue formula.
The amount left after costs should change
by exactly the amount we added or
removed. This is another valuable test because
it checks the relationship between controls, not
just one output value.
You can do the same with gross
margin. Moving the margin slider should affect
the result after costs, but it should
not change the number of orders.
If everything on a dashboard moves whenever
any slider changes, that may be a
sign that the model is not separating
its variables properly.
Understanding these relationships makes you a better
reviewer of generated tools.
The export button turns the scenario table
into a spreadsheet-friendly file.
Open that file and compare its rows
with the screen before sharing it.
Include the assumptions in the surrounding discussion,
because a table without context can easily
be mistaken for a forecast.
You may also want the tool to
export a timestamp and the input values
so a teammate can reproduce the calculation
later. One improvement I would request next
is sensitivity analysis: show which assumption has
the largest effect within a clearly defined
range. But I would not ask the
AI to invent a business stability score
without defining what the score means and
how it is validated.
More numbers do not automatically create more
insight. A small model with visible assumptions
is often more useful than a complicated
dashboard whose reasoning nobody can explain.

08-packaging.name: 08-packaging
08-packaging.title: Packaging: explore the concept
captions: Our fourth example moves from numbers to
a product concept.
Imagine that you need to discuss packaging
with a designer or supplier, but your
ideas are scattered across messages and rough
notes. A small interactive concept sheet can
bring the dimensions, material choice, color, and
review notes together.
The purpose is to improve the discussion,
not to pretend that a generated drawing
is ready to manufacture.
Start with the product name and the
three dimensions. We use millimetres throughout the
example, because mixing units is an easy
way to create confusion.
Change the width and watch both the
displayed specification and the drawing update.
The drawing is an illustrative unfolded arrangement
of panels, and it is intentionally labelled
as a concept.
It does not include every manufacturing detail
a real packaging engineer would need.
That limitation is important.
A production dieline may need material thickness,
fold allowances, glue tabs, tolerances, bleed, safety
margins, and supplier-specific requirements.
You cannot assume those details are correct
simply because a shape appears on screen.
The useful output here is a clear
starting point that makes it easier to
ask the right questions and compare alternatives.
Now try a different product name and
brand color. These are quick ways to
explore the visual direction without asking for
a new static image every time.
The interface gives you immediate feedback, and
you can keep the dimensions visible while
you experiment. That is helpful because a
design conversation often combines appearance and practical
constraints. The bill of materials is also
deliberately modest. It records the selected board
description, a simple print assumption, and an
insert that still needs to be specified
and tested. A placeholder is better than
an invented material specification.
If you do not know the answer
yet, make that uncertainty visible so somebody
can resolve it before production.
For a real project, I would add
constraints from the actual product and shipping
process. Does the package need to protect
fragile parts? Will it be stacked?
Does it need to fit a specific
mailing format? What is the expected quantity?
Those questions determine which features belong in
the next version of the tool.
They should come from the project rather
than from a model guessing what packaging
usually looks like.
The pattern is the same as the
earlier examples. We identify the inputs that
people keep changing, provide useful feedback, and
prepare an output that supports the next
action. In this case, the next action
is a review with the right person.
We will add a simple review state
and a printable handoff, while keeping the
boundary between concept review and production approval
explicit.

09-review-handoff.name: 09-review-handoff
09-review-handoff.title: Packaging: review and handoff
captions: Let’s make the review step visible.
Enter the reviewer’s name and mark the
concept as reviewed for discussion.
The wording matters.
This checkbox records a small local state
in the example; it is not a
digital signature, a supplier approval, or an
audit trail. Calling it approved for production
would make a much stronger claim than
the tool can support.
Try checking the box without a reviewer
name. The status should remain pending, because
a review with no identified reviewer is
not a useful handoff.
Then enter a name and check the
status again. These simple conditions are part
of the behavior we asked for, and
they are worth testing before we show
the tool to somebody else.
There is another important edge case.
What should happen if the dimensions change
after the review?
In a production workflow, the previous review
should no longer imply approval of the
changed specification. You would want a revision
number, a review date, and a clear
way to invalidate the old review when
relevant inputs change.
Our simple concept tool demonstrates the starting
point, and those are the next requirements
I would add before relying on it
with a team.
The print button lets you use the
browser’s print workflow to save a concept
sheet. Check the resulting document rather than
assuming that a good screen layout guarantees
a good printed page.
Look for clipped labels, missing dimensions, tiny
text, and content that lands on an
unexpected second page.
A handoff is only useful if the
recipient can actually read it.
You can also use this moment to
simplify. Not every control needs to appear
in the exported sheet.
The recipient probably needs the product name,
dimensions, material notes, revision, review status, and
the concept drawing.
They do not necessarily need the editing
controls or the prompt used to build
the app. Good outputs are designed around
the person who receives them.
This is why I like asking for
the export requirements early.
If the eventual output is a printable
specification, that shapes the interface differently from
a tool whose output is a message
or a spreadsheet.
The final handoff should not feel like
an afterthought attached to a pretty page.
Before moving on, notice how the four
examples have different outputs.
The newsletter produces content files, the task
board produces a draft message, the model
produces a scenario table, and the packaging
tool produces a concept sheet.
They share a method, but they are
not all the same app.
Start from the work and choose the
interface that helps that work move forward.
Next, we’ll apply the same thinking to
choosing ideas and preparing a presentation.

11-presentation.name: 11-presentation
11-presentation.title: Bonus: prepare a presentation
captions: Once an idea is selected, the next
request should describe the presentation’s job.
Do not start with make a beautiful
deck and hope the story appears.
Start with the audience, the decision you
want them to make, the evidence you
have, and the information that is still
uncertain. Design can make that story easier
to understand, but it cannot supply missing
evidence. For this example, we use a
six-part structure. First, describe the audience’s problem.
Second, explain the proposed approach.
Third, show a concrete example.
Fourth, identify the evidence needed to judge
the proposal. Fifth, describe the next steps.
Finally, state the decision you are asking
for. This is a practical outline, not
a universal formula, and you should change
it if your audience needs a different
sequence. Take our selected idea about turning
meeting notes into reviewed actions.
The problem is not simply that meetings
exist. The problem is that decisions and
responsibilities can become unclear afterward.
The proposed approach is a small workflow
that extracts a draft, asks a person
to review it, and produces a usable
handoff. The example should show what that
handoff looks like, using sample information rather
than private meeting notes.
The evidence slide is where we resist
the temptation to invent a success story.
If we have not measured time saved
or error rates, those are things to
test. We can propose a small trial
and define what we would observe, but
we should not present imagined results as
facts. A credible proposal makes the boundary
between evidence and assumption easy to see.
The next steps should also be concrete.
Choose a small pilot, identify who reviews
the output, decide where the reviewed actions
go, and agree on how to evaluate
the result. Then the final decision can
be specific: approve the pilot, choose an
owner, or resolve a particular question.
A presentation that ends with a vague
thank you may leave the audience unsure
what happens next.
Our tutorial tool lets you inspect that
outline and export the content for a
presentation workflow. When a real slide file
is created, open it in the application
where it will be presented and check
the actual slides.
Confirm that the text is readable, the
content is editable where needed, and nothing
runs off the edges.
A successful export message is not a
visual review. The larger lesson is that
interfaces should connect steps.
Idea selection leads to a shortlist, the
shortlist leads to an outline, and the
outline leads to a decision.
You can automate parts of that chain
without surrendering the judgment that makes the
result useful. Keep the human review at
the points where context, evidence, and responsibility
matter most.

12-building-better.name: 12-building-better
12-building-better.title: Build better tools
captions: Let’s bring the method together so you
can use it on your own task.
Start by describing the repeated work in
plain language. Who performs it, what information
do they begin with, and what usable
result should exist at the end?
If you cannot answer those questions yet,
a more elaborate interface probably will not
solve the uncertainty.
A small written example is a good
place to start.
Then identify the inputs that change.
In our newsletter, the text changes.
In the task board, the assignments and
estimates change. In the revenue model, the
assumptions change. In the packaging concept, the
dimensions and material notes change.
Those variables are strong candidates for controls
because you are likely to adjust them
repeatedly. Next, specify the output.
Be concrete about the format and the
person receiving it.
A downloadable file, a reviewed message, a
scenario table, and a printable sheet have
different requirements. Ask for a working output,
then test the actual result.
This single habit catches many problems that
remain invisible when you only look at
the page. After that, write two or
three small checks.
Use examples whose answers you already know.
Ten words should count as ten words.
Moving a thirty-minute task should transfer thirty
minutes between columns.
Two percent of twenty thousand should produce
four hundred. A review without a reviewer
should stay pending.
These checks turn a vague judgment about
whether the app feels right into something
more concrete. When you request a change,
describe the current behavior and the desired
behavior. For example, say that the review
remains checked after the dimensions change, and
ask for changes to invalidate that review.
That is easier to act on than
saying make the app smarter.
If a build is going in the
wrong direction, steer it toward the requirement
you actually need instead of letting unnecessary
features accumulate. Keep a copy of the
working version before a major change.
You want to be able to compare
the new behavior with the previous result.
A local project with version history is
useful for this, while a web artifact
can be convenient for quickly exploring an
idea. Choose the environment according to the
work, and do not assume that a
workflow is better merely because it looks
more technical. Finally, decide when the tool
is good enough for its intended use.
A personal prototype with sample data has
different requirements from a team tool that
stores customer information or sends messages.
Add the necessary permissions, storage rules, error
handling, and review steps before expanding its
responsibility. Small useful tools are powerful precisely
because you can understand them.
Preserve that clarity as they grow, and
let the next real problem guide the
next improvement.

p-opening.name: p-opening
p-opening.title: Build tools with AI
captions: What if the answer from
your AI was something
you could actually use?
Instead of copying
another wall of text,
imagine editing your
newsletter, moving tasks
around, testing business
assumptions, and
reviewing a product
concept right on the
screen.
In this tutorial, I’m
going to walk you
through those workflows
using practical
examples, and I’ll show
you how to check that
the tools work before
you trust them.

p-newsletter.name: p-newsletter
p-newsletter.title: Edit. Preview. Export.
captions: Let’s start with a
newsletter editor,
because it gives us a
simple way to understand
inputs, live feedback,
and a useful export.

p-tasks.name: p-tasks
p-tasks.title: Decide what happens next
captions: Now let’s apply the same
idea to a task list,
where the goal is to
decide what happens next
and make delegation
easier.

p-revenue.name: p-revenue
p-revenue.title: Make assumptions visible
captions: Next, we’ll build a
transparent revenue
model, change the
assumptions, and check
the calculations with
numbers we can verify
ourselves.

p-packaging.name: p-packaging
p-packaging.title: Explore before production
captions: Our fourth example is a
packaging concept, where
a useful interface helps
us explore ideas and
prepare a clear review,
without pretending the
result is ready for
manufacturing.

p-bonus.name: p-bonus
p-bonus.title: From ideas to decisions
captions: Finally, we’ll look at
how to turn these small
tools into a repeatable
way of working,
including idea selection
and a presentation
handoff.

p-closing.name: p-closing
p-closing.title: Build one useful tool
captions: Pick one task you repeat
every week, give it a
clear input and a useful
output, and test the
smallest version first.
The working examples and
prompts will accompany
this tutorial, so you
can adapt them to your
own workflow.

10-ideas.title: Bonus: choose an idea
captions: The bonus example is about making a
decision from a list of ideas.
A chat can give you many possible
titles, topics, or book concepts, but a
long list is not the same as
a choice. Once you have the candidates,
it can be more useful to give
each one a clear decision: keep it,
revisit it, or reject it.
The interface helps you compare the options
and keep a record of what you
decided. For this demonstration, the ideas are
sample entries that you can edit.
The local tool is not secretly calling
a model every time you click.
If you want fresh ideas, you can
ask an AI to generate candidates using
your audience, goals, constraints, and examples, then
bring the candidates into the decision tool.
Separating generation from selection makes it easier
to see which part of the process
needs improvement. Start with an idea that
has a specific audience and outcome.
A title like practical AI is broad.
A concept about helping a small service
business turn meeting notes into reviewed action
lists gives us more to evaluate.
We can ask who would use it,
what problem it addresses, and what evidence
we have that the problem matters.
The best choice is not necessarily the
one with the most dramatic title.
Now keep one idea, mark another for
later, and reject one that does not
fit the audience.
The selected list should update immediately.
You can use a swipe-style interaction if
it is convenient, but visible buttons are
important too. They make the choices understandable
and easier to use with a keyboard.
An interaction should help the decision rather
than making the tool harder to operate.
The useful next step is to add
a reason. Perhaps we kept an idea
because we can demonstrate it with real
examples. Perhaps we postponed another because the
supporting research is incomplete.
Those notes stop the shortlist from becoming
another unexplained list that somebody has to
interpret later. Export the shortlist so it
can leave the tool.
If the only copy of your decision
lives in a temporary page, you have
not finished the workflow.
A plain text export is enough for
a first version.
Later, you could add a more structured
format if it helps a real downstream
task. This idea-selection pattern works beyond content
planning. You could compare feature proposals, workshop
topics, or questions for customer interviews.
The categories and criteria should change with
the task, but the principle stays the
same: use the AI to help create
possibilities, then build a clear process for
evaluating them. In the next step, we’ll
take one selected idea and turn it
into a presentation that supports an actual
decision.
